# Generator-shortcuts answer

The original strongest shortcut was **bounding-box thickness**. Version 3.0.0 repaired it with irregular L-tailed components, but its palette still exposed two equally plausible canonical-fitting shortcuts: **one object per non-background color** and **every nonzero cell is foreground**. Those shortcuts avoid learning that the Racket authority first forms a binary mask in which both 0 and 9 are background and color changes do not split connected foreground.

The combined exact witness is retained in `repo/generators/2c4efc97c37d/counterexamples/binary-mask-shortcuts.json`. From left to right it contains a thin L-shaped component, a disconnected component reusing color 2, one connected component containing colors 4 and 5, and an isolated color-9 background cell. The intended result is `[[1,2,3]]`. Bounding-box thickness predicts `[[2,2,3]]`, one-object-per-color predicts `[[2,2,1]]`, and nonzero-foreground predicts `[[1,2,3,1]]`.

`workspace/onion_probe.py` computes all four outputs independently. The staged Racket test executes the selected canonical rule on this witness, canonical examples, generated examples, and exact boundary overrides. The final strict semantic gate accepted 600/600 draws, observed all three witnesses in 600/600, verified each rival claim 60/60, accepted 12/12 lessons, and found 0/48 ambiguous query rotations.

Yes, version 3.1.0 emits distinguishing cases by default. Even sample indices use disconnected unequal-depth components sharing a color; odd indices use a connected multicolor component; every draw has one isolated 9. A 512-case exact-axis census covered both modes equally with no failures. This finite evidence covers the three declared executable rivals, not every possible morphology or schedule-specific hypothesis.
